summary:
Putrajaya, a federal territory of Malaysia, stands under the national framework: Malaysia criminalises both same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at federal level, and the territory's own Sharia code adds a second layer that reaches Muslims only.

Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of "gross indecency" with up to 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping. These provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Sharia enactments in all 13 states and in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", carrying penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences reach Muslims only, they contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing, and enforcement sits with the state Islamic religious departments.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded in Malaysia. There is no same-sex marriage, and no federal law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.

Raids are the principal documented exposure. In October 2022 police raided a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur and arrested at least 20 LGBT people, and an August raid on an LGBT venue detained twenty men. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B in the largest operation of its kind since 2022; media were pre-tipped, detainees' faces and personal details were leaked, and 31 foreign nationals were held until their embassies intervened.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months, and documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked.

Litigation has narrowed the Sharia layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional, while the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact.

Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects.
tangentialFactors:
The Human Rights Watch report of 10 August 2022, "I Don't Want to Change Myself — Anti-LGBT Conversion Practices, Discrimination, and Violence in Malaysia", drew on interviews with 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 and documents state religious authorities harassing LGBT activists and organisations and raiding private events. It records the federal penal code punishing oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison and government-run "rehabilitation" programmes that at least 1,733 people had attended as of June 2021.

Enforcement since the 2018 election has been sustained and public. Beyond the Kuala Lumpur raids, a Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned, and in November 2023 Johor announced plans for conversion-therapy centres. These are single state-level data points illustrating a nationwide pattern rather than isolated incidents.

In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue a trans woman for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection. A constitutional challenge to the cross-dressing prohibition was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid after the November 2025 sauna raid, in which a magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point and 17 civil servants among those suspended. On 2 December 2025 the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.
localsOnly:
Residents who are Muslim fall under both layers. The Sharia cross-dressing offence applies to them regardless of where they are in the federation, and it is enforced by the state Islamic religious departments rather than the police, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Three of the 13 states also bar women from posing as men.

Malaysia operates a dual court system in which Sharia jurisdiction reaches Muslims only, while the federal Penal Code applies to everyone. Legal gender recognition is unavailable to residents as well as visitors, so documents cannot be brought into line with a person's lived gender.

Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and conversion-oriented provision is an established feature of state policy, with Johor announcing conversion-therapy centres in November 2023. LGBT events and media content are censored, no anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no same-sex marriage.

Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported, with transgender people particularly vulnerable. Documentation of the June 2019 killing of a trans woman in Klang records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources report no Putrajaya-specific enforcement case beyond the framework itself; the documented raids and arrests are recorded in Kuala Lumpur and other states. Whether enforcement in Putrajaya follows the same raid pattern is unresolved.

Whether Putrajaya's own Sharia enactment carries the same three-year, RM5,000 and six-stroke maximums stated for the general pattern across states and federal territories is not separately sourced. The inventory also does not state whether Putrajaya bars women from posing as men, a provision three states are recorded as having.

The outcome of the constitutional challenge pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women is not sourced here. Whether the November 2025 sauna raid operation extended beyond Kuala Lumpur and Penang is likewise unresolved.

Human Dignity Trust's profile was last updated 16 December 2025; no later legal change to the Penal Code or to Putrajaya's Sharia enactments is recorded in the inventory.
